extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions (administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decisionmakers, and advisors) and their legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for how postsecondary institutions must structure grievance procedures under Title IX—especially procedures for questioning parties and witnesses, assessing credibility, advisor participation, and limits on questions in live hearings and individual meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker must be able to assess credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution must ensure that the process it adopts under §106.46(f)(1) enables a decisionmaker to adequately assess the credibility of parties and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes for questioning (live hearings or individual meetings) must be structured to permit credibility-assessing questioning, and information gathered in such meetings becomes part of the evidence/investigative record to the extent relevant and permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual individual meetings permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations precludes a recipient from conducting individual meetings with parties and witnesses virtually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual meetings must use technology enabling the decisionmaker or investigator and the party or witness to simultaneously see and hear one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of individual meetings (before access to evidence/report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual meetings occur before the parties receive access to the evidence or investigative report; information gathered in these meetings is part of the evidence or investigative report under §106.46(e)(6)(i) to the extent relevant and not otherwise impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions have discretion whether individual meetings occur at the same time as or separate from investigative interviews, but the meetings' information is integrated into the investigative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for questioning in live hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: When an institution chooses to conduct a live hearing under §106.46(g), the process must allow the decisionmaker to ask relevant, non-impermissible questions and follow-ups, and either: (a) allow each party to propose questions to be asked by the decisionmaker (if not unclear or harassing), or (b) allow each party's advisor to ask such questions (if not unclear or harassing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions are not required to permit advisor-conducted questioning; they may choose either model. The decisionmaker remains responsible for conducting and overseeing the hearing even when advisors ask questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate questioning methods when no live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.46(f)(1)(i) governs when an institution does not conduct a live hearing: individual meetings with an investigator or decisionmaker, and a process allowing each party to propose questions to be asked by the investigator or decisionmaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department added §106.46(f)(1)(i)(C) requiring each party to receive a recording or transcript of any individual meetings with parties or witnesses, with enough time for the party to have a reasonable opportunity to propose follow-up questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent method within a particular complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution must use the same method for assessing credibility for each party or witness within resolution of a particular complaint (absent a party's need for a disability or language-access accommodation or auxiliary aids/services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions are not required to use the same method across all live hearings, but must articulate consistent principles in written grievance procedures explaining when different methods will apply and must treat parties equitably under §106.45(b)(1). Example: use advisor-questioning only for complaints with maximum sanctions of suspension/expulsion, with other complaints using decisionmaker-questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: No personal cross-examination by parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an institution uses a live hearing with questioning by an advisor, parties are never permitted to personally cross-examine each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition is explicitly included in §106.46(f)(1)(ii)(B) and reflects the policy that questioning must be conducted by the decisionmaker or an advisor, not by the parties themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide an appointed advisor only in specific circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement to provide an advisor for a party who does not have one (so the advisor can ask questions) applies only if the institution is using a live hearing with questioning by an advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions are not required to provide an advisor under other circumstances. When required to appoint an advisor, the institution must ensure the advisor can ask questions on the party's behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on advisor participation must apply equally
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.46(e)(2), a postsecondary institution may establish restrictions regarding the extent to which an advisor may participate in grievance procedures, provided the restrictions apply equally to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, an institution using live hearings without advisor questioning may limit an advisor's ability to speak during the live hearing; any limits must be equal for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appointing confidential employees as required advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: When an institution is required to appoint an advisor to ask questions on behalf of a party during advisor-conducted questioning, the institution may not appoint an individual who is currently a confidential employee or who received information as a confidential employee to serve as the advisor in that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is to avoid conflicts of interest. However, a party may still choose a confidential employee as their advisor of choice under §106.46(e)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to be accompanied by an advisor to any meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A party has the right to be accompanied to any meeting or proceeding by an advisor of their choice, regardless of whether the institution is using live hearings with questioning by an advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right applies to individual meetings under §106.46(f)(1)(i) and encompasses roles beyond questioning (e.g., support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker prescreens questions for relevance and impermissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisionmaker must determine whether a proposed question is relevant and not otherwise impermissible under §§106.2 and 106.45(b)(7) prior to the question being posed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescreening is consistent with the 2020 amendments and is intended to increase efficiency, reduce trauma, and prevent irrelevant/impermissible evidence from being introduced. Decisionmakers are trained on impartiality and on the meaning/application of 'relevant' and impermissible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker must explain exclusions for relevance or impermissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisionmaker is required to explain any decision to exclude a proposed question as not relevant or otherwise impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation helps guard against arbitrary exclusions; parties may appeal erroneous relevance determinations if they affected the outcome under §106.46(i)(1)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to clarify or revise unclear or harassing questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the decisionmaker determines a proposed question is unclear or harassing, the party must have an opportunity to clarify or revise the question and have the question asked if it is sufficiently clarified or revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers are not required to explain the rationale for exclusions based on 'unclear' or 'harassing.' The opportunity to revise ensures otherwise permissible questions are not excluded for poor wording or manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unclear or harassing questions applies to parties and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution must not permit questions that are unclear or harassing of the party or witness being questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prohibition can apply to both the content of a question and the manner in which it is asked; the Department declined to define 'unclear' or 'harassing' in regulatory text because determinations are fact-specific, but gave examples and context in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'relevant' added to §106.2 to guide prescreening
rubrics_metrics.description: To assist decisionmakers in making consistent determinations about excluding questions, the Department added a definition of 'relevant' to §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers receive training on the definition and on types of impermissible evidence to promote consistent rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical exclusions for certain sexual-history questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about the complainant's sexual interests are always excluded as impermissible; questions about the complainant's prior sexual conduct are excluded unless offered to prove someone other than the respondent committed the conduct or to prove consent where the prior sexual conduct was between the complainant and the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See §106.45(b)(7)(iii) for the regulatory text; whether other prior-conduct questions are harassing is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions may adopt and apply reasonable rules of decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Postsecondary institutions may 'adopt and apply other reasonable rules regarding decorum' for live hearings and proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such rules operate as a floor (not a ceiling); institutions may implement rules beyond those specified, but must apply them equally to both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable accommodations for disabilities during hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide reasonable accommodations and auxiliary aids/services to ensure full participation for people with disabilities in the live hearing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is required depends on the disability and circumstances (e.g., extra time to answer a question, particular means of answering). Recipients must comply with applicable disability laws; see discussion of §106.8(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: When credibility is in dispute standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements in §106.46(f)(1) to provide a process for questioning apply when credibility is in dispute and relevant to one or more allegations of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether credibility is in dispute is fact-specific; examples where credibility is not in dispute include respondent admissions or cases decided on non-testimonial evidence; courts have held cross-examination unnecessary when credibility is not at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to make prior findings that credibility is in dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution is not required to make specific findings on whether credibility is in dispute and relevant prior to cross-examination of each witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determination of dispute is fact-specific and need not be recorded as a separate finding before proceeding with questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights for erroneous relevance/procedure rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may appeal erroneous relevance determinations if they affected the outcome, under §106.46(i)(1)(i) (appeal rights include procedural irregularity that affected the outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appellate path serves as a check on decisionmaker exclusions that materially impacted the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to respond to questions — contested approaches and considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: There was significant commentary on proposed §106.46(f)(4) regarding whether a decisionmaker should disregard prior supportive statements of a party who refuses to answer credibility-related questions; commenters offered alternative approaches (consider prior statements in totality, weigh refusal under totality of circumstances), and raised concerns about chilling reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department summarized varied opinions and suggested alternatives (e.g., allow decisionmaker discretion to weigh evasiveness or refusal), noting competing concerns about fairness and chilling effects; this is an area of debated procedural approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions may outsource investigations/adjudications but remain responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients remain free to consider alternate investigation and adjudication models (including regional centers) that outsource functions to outside experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if functions are outsourced, the recipient (institution) remains responsible for ensuring its grievance procedures comply with §106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement for impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.8(d)(2) requires all investigators, decisionmakers, and other individuals responsible for implementing a postsecondary institution's grievance procedures to be trained on how to serve impartially, including avoiding prejudgment, conflicts of interest, and bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers' training supports prescreening and impartial exclusion/explanation duties and helps guard against arbitrary exclusions of questions or evidence.
